records.sourceFile: Oxygen straight to the brain - An overview of hyperbaric oxygen therapy for a variety of brain morbidities.pdf

paper.citation: Leighton T, VanHorne E, Parsons D. Oxygen Straight to the Brain: An Overview of Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy for a Variety of Brain Morbidities. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2024;23(4):130-136.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers hyperbaric oxygen therapy as an off-label treatment for traumatic brain injury, posttraumatic stress disorder and migraine. For each condition it reviews the pathological mechanisms and then the HBOT treatment targets and reported effects. The authors identify a lack of consistent patient selection and treatment timing as a shared shortfall and call for further research.
paper.tldr: A narrative review of hyperbaric oxygen for prolonged concussion symptoms, PTSD and migraine, built mainly on military and veteran studies. Short-term benefits are reported in some studies, but protocols are not standardized and the authors do not support it as a routine treatment.
paper.methods: Narrative review organized by condition (TBI and postconcussion syndrome, PTSD, migraine). The paper does not describe a search strategy, study selection or quality appraisal.
paper.findings: For TBI, the most favorable results came from 1.3 to 1.5 ATA for 60 minutes daily for 2 to 4 weeks, while pressures above 2.0 ATA were much less effective for mild TBI postconcussion symptoms; imaging studies linked cognitive gains after HBOT to metabolic changes in specific brain regions. For PTSD, a veteran case-control pilot reported that 12 of 23 subjects (52%) no longer met PTSD criteria after 40 sessions, and a sham-controlled trial in military personnel with mild TBI found a PCL-C change of -9.3 versus 3.0 with sham at week 13 that did not persist at 6 and 12 months. For migraine, the evidence was rated low quality, HBOT did not reduce rescue or abortive medication use, and the authors conclude that long-term HBOT for migraine cannot be supported.
paper.limitations: No search method is described, and the cited studies have small samples, poor follow-up, subjective outcome reporting and confounding comorbidities such as TBI, depression, anxiety and polypharmacy. None of the cited HBOT studies are in athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: The review does not support HBOT as a routine treatment for concussion, PTSD or migraine. It notes that standard concussion care is initial rest followed by daily activities, mild aerobic exercise and gradual progression, and that HBOT carries risks (barotrauma, oxygen toxicity, worsening cataracts) and substantial cost (about $160 to $200 per hour, with 40 sessions often recommended).
paper.athleteDev: The review does not address athletic performance or training, so it cannot inform performance programming.
paper.rtp: The review discusses prolonged postconcussion symptoms but gives no return-to-sport criteria, and its HBOT evidence comes from military and veteran samples. It cannot be used to clear an athlete for return to play or to justify HBOT as part of a concussion return-to-sport plan.

records.sourceFile: Public chronic traumatic encephalopathy knowledge - Sources, accuracy and confidence.pdf

paper.citation: Zurlinden T, Falletta G, Schneider K, Sorrell AE, Savransky A, Everhart DE. Public Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Knowledge: Sources, Accuracy and Confidence. Current Sports Medicine Reports. 2024;23(1):23-28.
paper.abstract: The survey measured public knowledge of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the sources people use, their confidence in that knowledge, and their comfort allowing a child to play a high-contact sport. Average accuracy was 48%, and the most common errors concerned the cause and diagnosis of CTE. Confidence was linked with comfort about children playing high-contact sport, but accuracy was not.
paper.tldr: Members of the public in this survey were often wrong about CTE, especially its cause and how it is diagnosed, and their confidence was unrelated to their accuracy, yet more confident people were more comfortable letting children play high-contact sport. Television, movies and professional athletes were weakly linked with more accurate knowledge, and social media with less accurate knowledge.
paper.methods: An online survey of 530 participants was analysed, with 529 reported in the abstract and in Table 1. Participants answered six true/false CTE knowledge items (two taken from Merz et al. and four written from the Sports Neuropsychology Society fact sheet), rated their confidence and comfort on 0 to 100 scales, and estimated the share of their CTE information from each source. Total accuracy and item-level accuracy were calculated, and correlations were used to relate sources, confidence, accuracy and comfort.
paper.findings: Average CTE knowledge accuracy was 48.02%; only 33.01% correctly rated that CTE cannot be caused by a single injury, 33.97% that it cannot develop without a head injury and 33.21% that it can be diagnosed only after death, while 70.69% correctly said it cannot be treated. Confidence was not related to accuracy (r = -0.040, p = 0.385) but was positively correlated with comfort allowing a child to play high-contact sport (r = 0.199, p <= 0.001), while accuracy was not (r = 0.004). Television/movies (r = 0.088) and professional athletes (r = 0.127) were weakly linked with higher accuracy, and social media with lower accuracy (r = -0.181).
paper.limitations: Participants were self-selected online volunteers, and the authors could not control for health literacy, English literacy or computer access. 9.26% of the sample said they had never heard of CTE but still had to answer true or false, so accuracy near 50% may partly reflect guessing. The text gives 529 participants in the abstract and Table 1 but 530 in the Methods, and the Discussion's 68.90% believing sport alone causes CTE does not match Table 2 (33.97% correct, about 66% wrong).
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians and sport staff should correct common CTE misconceptions when they talk with athletes and families, especially that CTE comes from a single injury or from sport alone, and that it can be diagnosed in life. Because confidence was not linked with accuracy, staff should not assume that a parent's certainty about CTE reflects correct knowledge.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: This study does not measure training or performance. Its practical value for performance and medical staff is in education, since the authors suggest that clinicians and staff raise CTE facts with athletes and families when sport participation is discussed.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It surveys members of the public about CTE and reports no injured athletes, concussion management or return-to-play outcomes.

records.sourceFile: The Association Between Age of First Exposure to American Football at a Young Age and Later-Life Health Issues in Healthy, Community-Dwelling Adults.pdf

paper.citation: Rigney GH, Dugan JE, Bishay A, Jonzzon S, Jo J, Williams KL, et al. The association between age of first exposure to American football at a young age and later-life health issues in healthy, community-dwelling adults. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: In 107 former amateur American football players, starting to play before age 12 was not associated with depressive, anxiety, neurobehavioral, cognitive, general health, motor or functional outcomes after adjustment. A greater number of lifetime concussions was associated with worse psychiatric, cognitive and neurobehavioral scores.
paper.tldr: Among healthy former amateur players, starting football before age 12 was not linked to worse later-life mood, cognition or health scores after adjustment, but more self-reported lifetime concussions were. Use this as evidence that concussion burden matters, not as a green light for early tackling.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey of men with at least one year of amateur American football participation who were recruited through the ResearchMatch registry. Multivariable linear and logistic regressions adjusted for age, number of lifetime concussions and total years of football for depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), neurobehavioral symptoms (NSI), cognitive complaints (BC-CCI), and general health, motor and functional outcomes.
paper.findings: Of 107 analysed men (41 with age of first exposure under 12, 66 with 12 or older), age of first exposure under 12 did not predict PHQ-9 (B = 0.51, p = 0.682), GAD-7 (B = 0.09, p = 0.926), NSI (B = -0.56, p = 0.850) or BC-CCI (B = -0.65, p = 0.403), and results were unchanged with age of first exposure as a continuous variable. Each additional lifetime concussion was associated with higher PHQ-9 (B = 0.44), GAD-7 (B = 0.33), NSI (B = 1.04) and BC-CCI (B = 0.26) scores, all p < 0.001, and with higher odds of sleep problems (OR 1.30) and chronic pain (OR 1.91). Unadjusted comparisons showed higher PHQ-9 and GAD-7 scores, more current depression (29.3% versus 13.6%) and more sleep problems (p = 0.050) in the under-12 group, but these were not significant once age, concussions and years of play were adjusted for.
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional, self-report design cannot show cause, and recall of exposure and concussions may be inaccurate. Participants were registry volunteers, mostly white and college-educated, and only those with complete surveys and no neurological disease were analysed. The under-12 group was small and younger, and other contact sport exposure was not adjusted for. The text and Table 2 disagree on years of football in the under-12 group (5.0 versus 5.1 years; p = 0.021 versus p < 0.001), the Table 1 concussion counts for the under-12 group do not add up to 41, and the abstract conclusion calls the sample 'young' despite a mean age of 60.6; table values are reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: This study does not show that starting football before age 12 is safe or unsafe. The association between more lifetime concussions and worse mood, cognitive, sleep and pain scores supports keeping an accurate concussion history for each player. Explain to parents that the study cannot answer their question about long-term risk of early starts.
paper.athleteDev: For medical and performance staff, the study supports recording each athlete's full concussion history. It does not address on-field performance, and it does not identify a safe starting age for football.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It surveyed generally healthy former players about lifetime concussions and later symptoms, not recovery from a current injury. Its link between concussion count and later symptoms should not be used to set return-to-play timelines.
